Awka: Department of Linguistics, Nnamdi Azikiwe University. Companion: Anagbogu, Philip N. 2006. The numerical system of Koring: An analysis. AJILL 2(1): 71-75 (endnote 2, p. 75).
catalog_locator: pp. 119-120; companion tone convention: Anagbogu 2006 numerals, p. 75, endnote 2
catalog_quote: In Anagbogu (2003b), it is shown that deverbal nominals are derivable from monosyllabic, disyllabic and trisyllabic verb root bases. All the various manifestations of tonal behaviour associated with those formations form the basis for postulating tone rules, summarized below: (i) The tone of the verb root determines that of the prefix in derivations involving monosyllabic verb root bases ... (ii) The prefixation of the nominalizing morpheme raises the tone of the vowels in the base of disyllabic verb roots to high if they are low ... but root vowels with high tones remain invariable tonally ... (iii) The rule for trisyllabic roots is that the last two syllables of the derivative become high-toned. The prefix then assimilates in tone to the immediately following syllable. ... In the rest of the work, high tones are unmarked, low tones are marked / / while downstep is marked with a macron.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

All the various manifestations of tonal behaviour associated with those formations form the basis for postulating tone rules, summarized below: (i) The tone of the verb root determines that of the prefix in derivations involving monosyllabic verb root bases" followed by examples (1) mzo 'pray' < mlezo 'prayer', (2) kal 'judge' < kekal 'judgment', then rules (ii) L-to…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states anything about word stress. Koring is described as a tone language with high and low tones plus downstep (H unmarked, L grave, downstep macron), with tone rules in nominalization and compounding (e.g. the verb root's tone determines the nominalizing prefix's tone; disyllabic low-toned roots become high under nominalization; in trisyllabic derivatives the last two syllables become high and the prefix assimilates). Anagbogu 2005:132 speaks of 'the stability of tone' across dialects; Anagbogu 2006 (numerals) endnote 2, p. 75: 'Tonal convention: The high tone is left unmarked throughout, while low tone is marked with / ` / and the downstep is marked with / ¯ /.' Nkamigbo 2015 (syllable structure, OT) tone-marks its data but never mentions tone or stress in prose.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None relevant to stress. Tone rules: high-toned root vowels remain invariant under nominalization (2006a:120); third-person plural subject vs object pronouns differ only in downstep vs low tone on the final vowel (2005:137).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical/morphological tone on words (nominalizations, compounds, reduplicated adverbs/nouns/verbs/adjectives with patterns like LL-LL, HH-HH, LL-HH); word level, elicited from Okpoto-dialect informants; no phrase-level prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand Koring data opened (Anagbogu 2005, 2006a, 2006b; Nkamigbo 2015) are from the Okpoto dialect (Ishielu LGA, Ebonyi State), which Nkamigbo 2015:44 calls the widely recognised standard dialect; other dialects are Ntezi, Effium, Amuda, Ufia/Utonkon, Ufiom and the Wanishan variety at Okpoma. Glottolog has no separate dialect codes under orin1239 that I could confirm.

sources.note: Nothing on stress. States tone rules for nominalizations (root tone determines prefix tone; L roots raised to H; trisyllabic derivatives LHH) and the convention H unmarked / L grave / downstep macron (p. 120); tonal patterns of reduplicated forms LL-LL, HH-HH, LL-HH, HH-LH (pp. 127-128). Scanned PDF, scanned; quotes checked on page scan. Reference list names Anagbogu 2004 'An introduction to the phonology of Koring' (Ihafa, Lagos, forthcoming), 2003a/b, 2005a/b, 2006 orthography, 2007 dictionary.
